## Rhythm before there are any pitches

You can write down a rhythm before you have chosen a single note. A list of
durations already tells you where the attacks fall, how long the whole phrase
runs, and which spans feel stretched or hurried against the beat underneath.
Take the tune away and the rhythm is still recognisable. Tap out the opening of
anything you know well, with no pitches at all, and somebody in the room will
name it.

Sonic Pi makes that list executable, because `sleep` accepts fractional beats.
One number per event, and the program is a rhythm.

Before the code, one convention has to be nailed down, since the traditional
names carry a division in them that has nothing to do with clock time. In this
book a *quarter note* lasts 1 beat. An eighth note lasts `0.5`. A sixteenth
note lasts `0.25`. Those fractions divide the quarter-note beat, and they say
nothing at all about seconds. Change `use_bpm` and every one of them changes
duration in milliseconds while the written rhythm stays exactly as it was. That
separation is worth holding on to. Notation describes proportion; tempo turns
proportion into time.

The renderer below takes a duration array and one percussion sample. Every
attack has the identical colour, so nothing distinguishes the events except
where they land. Clap the whole beat along with it and keep that beat moving
underneath the smaller values. When your clap loses its place, note which
subdivision broke it, the half-beat or the quarter-beat.

## Seven attacks, one drum

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96

durations = [1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 1]

define :play_rhythm do |lengths, sound|
  lengths.each do |duration|
    sample sound, amp: 0.9, finish: [duration * 0.35, 1].min
    sleep duration
  end
end

puts "#{durations.sum} beats"
play_rhythm durations, :drum_tom_mid_soft
```

One drum colour, seven attacks. The first takes a whole beat on its own. Two
half-beat gaps split the beat that follows. Then the pair of quarter-beat
values compresses the middle, another half beat opens it back out, and a final
whole beat closes the phrase. The log prints the total span. Pitch, sample and
amplitude never move, so every change in density comes from the array.

## Predict the sum before you run it

1. Replace every `0.5` with `0.25`. More attacks now fit into less musical
   time, so the phrase gets shorter and its centre gets busier. Work out the
   new total on paper first, then check yourself against the log.

2. Restore the durations and change only the sample. Pick one with a long tail
   and try to locate the same seven onsets. How much harder did that get, and
   did the score change at all?

3. Back to the original sample. Alter one duration and predict the new printed
   total before you press Run. Confirm that the total and the onset pattern
   moved together, because they're two views of one edit.

## Onsets are prefix sums

Durations build a timeline by addition, and two sums matter. Add all of them
and you have the phrase length. Add everything before a given event and you
have that event's onset, which programmers know as a prefix sum. Take `[1, 0.5,
0.5]`: the attacks land at beats 0, 1 and 1.5, and the span is 2 beats. That
arithmetic is the entire scheduling model of this renderer.

The familiar subdivisions fall straight out of it. Two eighth-note values of
`0.5` fill the same beat as one quarter-note value of `1`, and four
sixteenth-note values of `0.25` fill it too. Which means the array is
self-checking in a way notation is not: if a bar is supposed to be four beats
and the numbers sum to 3.75, you have a bug you can see before you hear it.

When your clapping goes uncertain, count the smallest subdivision out loud for
long enough to place every attack, then work back up. The goal is hearing those
small units inside the beat while the beat keeps running. A common failure is
letting the subdivision replace the beat: you count sixteen fast pulses,
perfectly evenly, and lose all sense of which one was the downbeat.

Tempo enters only at the last moment, and it enters as a single multiplication.
At 96 BPM one beat lasts 625 milliseconds, so the `0.25` values in this array
occupy about 156 milliseconds each. Halve the tempo and every one of those
numbers doubles in duration while the array on screen sits unchanged. This is
why the durations are stored as beats and never as seconds. A rhythm written in
seconds stops being a rhythm the moment somebody wants it faster.

## What an array of durations can and cannot say

Because a rhythm is now data, you can check it and transform it before any
sound happens. Reject a bar whose sum is wrong. Double every value to augment
the rhythm, or halve them all to diminish it. Compute all the onsets and ask
whether anything lands on a beat. The renderer needs to know none of this. It
advances by whatever duration it's handed.

The format buys that simplicity by giving up something real. Each value serves
as the time until the next onset and, through `finish`, as part of the
articulation of the current sound. One number is doing two jobs. So this format
can't describe two notes that overlap while a third starts in the gap between
them. Later event scores split `:start` from `:duration` for exactly that
reason, and Lesson 14 takes the first step by giving every event an explicit
`:start` field. Here, sequential prefix sums are enough, and they keep the
arithmetic audible.

Keep sample length and rhythmic duration apart in your head. `finish` decides
how much of the recording you hear; `sleep duration` decides when the next
event fires. A short source can finish well before a one-beat value has
elapsed, leaving a hole. A long tail can still be ringing when the next attack
arrives, gluing two events together. Neither one moved an onset. When you're
checking rhythm, listen to the attack positions and treat the tail as
articulation, the same distinction you drew between `release` and `sleep` in
Lesson 7.

Lesson 13 fixes the subdivisions at equal length and adds recurring accents on
top of them. The duration sum will define how much time a bar occupies; the
accents will tell your ear how that time is grouped.

## Write a rhythm interpreter

Write an interpreter that takes a duration array and a sample symbol. Build two
patterns out of quarter-, eighth- and sixteenth-note values, each adding up to
four beats, and have the program print the sum and refuse anything that isn't
four.

Then start a quiet click on every whole beat in a separate thread and clap each
pattern against it. Your renderer should swallow at least two different sample
symbols without a line changing inside its loop. While you audition in Sonic Pi
5, write down the first fractional value where your clap drifts away from the
click. That single observation tells you which subdivision you need to count
out loud rather than feel.
